To me the kibbutz seems like the most idealistic arrangement possible. You do something useful as well as you can, you're part of the collective, and you don't live ostentatiously. There's no time between jobs and no looking for work; you're always useful in one way or another. It sounds fantastic, but in modern Israel it has largely disappeared or been replaced. And of course that idealistic image hides some genuine weaknesses in the model.

But the kibbutz isn't the only model that's been proposed for how people can live in communities or societies without it being quite so brutal. In most of the world, for most people, either you work and earn your right to eat and have a home, or you live on welfare. There have been other versions of the basic social contract. What are some that have been proposed and actually put into practice, besides the kibbutz, including any modern successors?

I believe people need a baseline. Only when you know there's something under you can you reach your potential. Where housing is insecure, for example where rental tenancies can end at the landlord's will, people are never sure they'll have a stable home, and their first concern is keeping a roof over their heads. In a perverse sense, that makes us less evolved than our ancestors living in the jungle, who took care of their basic needs first and built on top of that. We've built supposedly advanced societies, yet the very foundation that human potential grows from, stable housing and a sense of purpose, has been made shaky.

Do we have to go all the way to the kibbutz to find a saner version of modern society? Or are there other real attempts we can point to, where people decided that pure capitalism is disastrous for society at large and built an alternative that actually works for the people living in it?

prompt: I'd love an episode on named entity recognition — NER. What are the classic NER programs and approaches, and how do they differ from the more modern ways of finding entities in a body of text? We've actually built this into the podcast: every episode now runs through an entity extraction step that pulls out the people, organisations, places and so on that get discussed, links them to Wikidata, and builds an entity index on the website. So I'm curious how these tools deal with the hard parts — the same name spelled different ways, aliases and transliterations, and disambiguation (two different things with the same name). And if you were building an NER pipeline today, what are the foundational models and tools you'd want to know about?
context: How MWP's own entity index works (PLAN-024, live since 2026-10-10): it is LLM-based, not a classic NER model. After each episode is finalised, an LLM (DeepSeek Flash) reads the script and extracts entities typed as person / org / place / work / event / product, each with a salience score (1 passing mention, 2 discussed, 3 episode topic) and the surface form as said. Linking: the LLM guesses a Wikipedia title, which is resolved to a Wikidata QID ("linked"); failing that, a Wikidata search returns the top 5 candidates and the LLM picks one ("provisional", worth spot-checking); otherwise "unlinked" (including when the only match is a disambiguation page or a family-name item). Dedupe is by Wikidata QID when there is one, else by type plus case-insensitive name/alias match, with an aliases list per entity. A later enrichment pass found and cleared wrong links — e.g. "Yachad" the Israeli political party had been linked to a disability charity of the same name, a live example of the disambiguation problem. Entity websites come only from Wikidata, never from an LLM.
